briefing.text: The hypothesis is about how tumoroids engrafted in mice respond to chemotherapy. Before any analysis, check whether the provided tables hold a measured drug-response variable at all. Grep every clinical column name and '#' description line, plus the other files, for terms such as respon, sensitiv, IC50, AUC, volume, xenograft, mouse, engraft, RECIST and TRG. A first library check found none. The tables appear to hold patient sex, sample-level therapy before derivation, site, MSI and TMB, plus mutations and CNA. Confirm this yourself.
briefing.reason: Whether the hypothesis can be tested depends on whether a response variable exists, so this check has to come first.

briefing.text: THERAPY_PRIOR_TO_DERIVATION in data_clinical_sample.txt records what treatment the patient received before the organoid was derived. It is blank for most of the roughly 340 samples; the rest hold FOLFOX/CRT/FOLFIRI/SCRT strings. It is not the organoid's or the mouse's response to chemotherapy. Do not use it as a response outcome. At most it is an exposure covariate.
briefing.reason: This is the column most easily mistaken for a chemotherapy-response variable.

briefing.text: Genomic heterogeneity across tumoroids (different KRAS/TP53/APC status, MSI, TMB) is not measured drug-response heterogeneity. Predicting sensitivity to 5-FU/oxaliplatin/irinotecan from mutations is weak and unvalidated in rectal cancer. Do not use genomic variation as evidence for or against 'uniform sensitivity'.
briefing.reason: This stops a team from using a genomic proxy in place of the response outcome.

briefing.text: Sample ID suffixes encode the material. '-pt' is the patient tumour and '-tm' is the tumoroid/organoid (Sample Type Unknown_Tumor, Fresh). IM3/IM5/IM6 are clinical MSK-IMPACT panels of patient tumours. The library counted about 21 pt, 31 tm and 287 IMPACT samples. Check whether any mouse or xenograft sample class exists. Genomic concordance between matched pt and tm samples shows the organoid represents its tumour; it says nothing about whether drug response is uniform.
briefing.reason: Teams need to know which samples are tumoroids, and should not read pt/tm concordance as response evidence.

briefing.text: In studies like this, in vivo chemo-response results (e.g. tumour volume in mice) usually sit in the paper's supplementary data, which is not provided. Base the label only on variables present in the given files. Do not fill in published findings from memory.
briefing.reason: This guards against importing outside knowledge of the study's results.

shared_assumptions: Both teams treated 'chemotherapy sensitivity' as needing an explicit response column (volume, IC50, RECIST) and did not consider whether the dataset design itself (paired patient -pt vs tumoroid -tm samples, treatment-labelled derivatives) encodes a treatment-response comparison.
Both assumed SAMPLE_CLASS='Tumor' for every row means no engrafted/mouse samples, without checking whether ID suffixes ('m' in P2m/P7m/P9m, MC/PC/TNT) are the in-mouse encoding.
unused_evidence: About 300 MSK-IMPACT clinical samples (P-xxxx-T0x IDs, SAMPLE_TYPE Primary/Metastasis, empty preservation field) form a separate clinical cohort; neither team said what it is for or whether it carries any clinical-response-like field relevant to the 'unlike clinical observations' part.

THERAPY_PRIOR_TO_DERIVATION differs between parent tumoroid and derivatives (e.g. 'none' -> 'FOLFOX', 'CRT' -> 'CRT + FOLFOX'); both teams saw it but did not tabulate all derivative lineages to establish what they represent.
Columns TISSUE_SITE ('na' on derivatives), SAMPLE_TYPE 'Unknown_Tumor' (6 rows) and the empty MSK_SLIDE_ID/PATH_SLIDE_EXISTS were not interpreted.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named the undocumented derivative suffixes (MC, PC, TNT, P2m/P7m/P9m) as weakest point and only reported it; neither checked how many derivatives exist, which parents they come from, or whether they are the engrafted/treated arm.
second_readings: 'Uniform sensitivity' could be read as a claim about whether treated derivatives of different tumoroids end up with uniform vs divergent states; the strict reading needs a measured response, which both teams found absent. Both readings point to the same variable gap only if no response proxy exists.
challenge.verdict: Fairly high trust in Not verifiable: I confirmed no response, volume or engraftment column exists in the clinical sample table. The remaining risk is the undocumented derivative suffixes and the unexplained clinical cohort, which neither team resolved.

In public cBioPortal-style datasets of patient-derived tumoroids/organoids, how are xenografted or in-mouse-treated derivatives typically encoded (SAMPLE_CLASS values, sample-ID suffix conventions), and is treatment response ever stored in clinical sample tables?
questions.why: Settles whether the absence of a SAMPLE_CLASS 'xenograft' value and of response columns really means no in vivo response data is encoded.

findings.question: In public cBioPortal-style datasets of patient-derived tumoroids/organoids, how are xenografted or in-mouse-treated derivatives typically encoded (SAMPLE_CLASS values, sample-ID suffix conventions), and is treatment response ever stored in clinical sample tables?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY THE WEB: all three research calls (two searches, one contents fetch of docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats) failed with HTTP 502 / Exa 403, so no page was read. From domain knowledge only: SAMPLE_CLASS is a free-text cBioPortal sample attribute (common values: Tumor, Cell line, Organoid, Xenograft). When PDX or in-mouse derivatives are deposited, they usually appear as separate samples with their own IDs or suffixes and a Xenograft-type class. Drug or treatment response is rarely put in clinical sample tables; it usually sits in the paper's supplementary material or in a separate timeline/treatment file. So if the data have no Xenograft class and no response column, they most likely encode no in vivo chemo-response, which points to Not verifiable.
